narrative:
The 2020 Minnesota Twins arrived at their abbreviated 60-game season as one of baseball's most anticipated teams, fresh off a record-setting home run campaign the year before. They opened July with a crisp 5-2 record, looking every bit the AL Central favorites they were supposed to be. But the first week of August told a different story, as closer Taylor Rogers — one of their most trusted arms — was torched in back-to-back appearances against Pittsburgh, surrendering crucial runs that foreshadowed the bullpen fragility lurking beneath the surface.

August proved to be a grind. The Twins went 15-14, a winning record that nonetheless felt like treading water. Their most impactful moments were almost exclusively painful: home runs surrendered by Trevor May, José Berríos, Jorge Alcala, and Tyler Duffey, and another late-game meltdown from Rogers against the White Sox. Yet through all of it, the rotation stayed largely intact, the offense kept churning out runs, and Minnesota did what good teams do in bad stretches — they survived.

September was where the Twins truly came alive. Going 16-8 in the season's final month, they looked like the contender everyone expected. Byron Buxton delivered a thunderous three-run homer in early August that hinted at what was coming, and in September the offense fully erupted. Miguel Sanó, Jorge Polanco, and Max Kepler delivered walk-off and late-inning heroics, capped by a dominant three-hit sequence against Detroit on September 22nd. The Twins had locked up the AL Central and looked dangerous heading into October.

But the postseason brought heartbreak, as it so often does in Minnesota. Facing the Houston Astros in the Wild Card round, the Twins traded blows across two games, with Nelson Cruz delivering a clutch double and Sergio Romo getting a key out — but the bullpen cracked at the worst moments. A bases-loaded walk from Romo blew the lead in Game 1, Michael Brantley's single salted the wound, and Carlos Correa's home run in Game 2 ended the series. The Twins' postseason curse — then 18 consecutive losses dating back years — extended once more, leaving a talented roster with nothing to show for a promising 36-24 campaign.

chapters.title: Fast Start, Then Trouble in the Bullpen
chapters.description: The Twins open strong in July before Taylor Rogers is burned twice in August, exposing early cracks in a team with championship hopes.

chapters.title: Buxton Sparks a Rally
chapters.description: Byron Buxton's three-run homer provides a jolt of energy as the Twins try to steady themselves amid a stretch of frustrating home runs allowed.

chapters.title: Winning Ugly Through August
chapters.description: Minnesota goes 15-14 on the month, surviving a parade of costly home runs surrendered by their bullpen to stay afloat in the AL Central race.

chapters.title: September Surge
chapters.description: The Twins catch fire in the final month, with Sanó, Polanco, Kepler, and Buxton delivering clutch hits in a dominant 16-8 stretch that cements the division title.

chapters.title: October Heartbreak
chapters.description: The Twins battle the Astros in the Wild Card round but fall apart in the bullpen, extending their agonizing postseason losing streak as the season ends in familiar disappointment.
